newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Lufthansa warned of wider stoppages.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Lufthansa warned of wider stoppages.

text.p: A German union said on Tuesday it was preparing a second and expanded wave of walkouts by employees over a pay dispute with German airline Deutsche Lufthansa AG.
The threat by the DAG white-collar union followed the breakdown on Monday of the latest round of wage talks.
Ground and air staff represented by DAG last month held brief stoppages that cost the airline some 12 million marks ($7.72 million), with 35 flights cancelled.

"We shall make it clear that our anger has become greater," a DAG official told Reuters, adding that a greater number of airports would be affected and that the walk-outs would stretch to the maximum two hours allowed by law.
Sources close to airline staff said the protests are likely to hit international traffic next time as well as the domestic airports involved in the first protest.
They added that if Lufthansa refused to change its position as a result, a ballot on all-out strike action could follow.

DAG, which shares representation of the airline's 50,000 staff with the transport and public sector union OeTV, has said Lufthansa has still not offered its members a 1997 wage increase in line with others in the industry.

It is also angry that Lufthansa wants the new contracts to last 27 months instead of a year. Given the threat that many Lufthansa jobs could be moved abroad, the union would not tie itself to a two-year contract, DAG has said.
Lufthansa in a statement called for DAG to come back to the negotiating table and call off the planned protests.
The DAG official said the new stoppages were certain to hit Frankfurt airport, the country's biggest, while Hamburg was also likely to be affected.

DAG represents the airline's pilots, flight attendants and other white collar workers. Other staff are represented by the OeTV union, which has agreed a wage deal with Lufthansa that the DAG rejected.

The two-year OeTV deal was reached in October and calls for workers to receive a one-off payment equal to one-third of a month's base pay. In addition, the airline said workers would receive a 1.7 percent pay rise in 1998.
The offer also included a one-off payment of either 500 marks in cash or 625 marks in Lufthansa stock as part of a unique profit-sharing scheme for a company that is still partially state-owned.
